sources.context: The longest first-person Rod Wave interview available anywhere: a 2h13m sit-down released two days before his seventh album. Quotations here are reproduced from YouTube's machine-generated transcript, which is unpunctuated, occasionally garbles words ('feel away' for 'feel a way') and does not label speakers; attributions were made from surrounding turn structure and every quotation used was checked for a coherent single-speaker run. Audio was not reviewed. Repair stage 2026-09-18: the verifier found C92 and the Type 4 FAQ used lines from the Lil Poppa answer (~101:41-108:45) as a present, unprompted self-description. sources.excerpt: 'I feel like I'm Rod Wave once out of here. And when it's time to drop an album, do a tour, then I'm back to normal living. And it really don't really hit me until it's time to drop albums or do tours or do press runs where I actually like remember who I am.' On his public image: 'I give them so little that they got to work with what they got... it's just not natural for me to push that on people or try to prove a point of who I am.' On the framing of his music: 'people always taking and saying pain like I'm still not even like that word... it's not pain, it's not sad, it's not — it's normal. It's reality.' Asked whether he has ever gone to therapy: 'Nah.' Asked 'Just straight music?': 'Straight music, man.' On betrayal: 'poverty is something like you born into... But betrayal is like a decision.' On peace: 'I'm in my big king bed... AC on 65... me and baby just kick back watching TV, laughing. That's when I be at real peace.' Additional passages used in the draft: 'the image that people got about me is totally different'; 'I wish people didn't you know what I'm saying take my image and run with it'; 'my hobby, my therapy'; asked '>> You've never been there.' he answers 'Yeah, been there.'; on Ari Lennox: 'There's some things I just don't got control over'; 'maybe that was like a management call'; 'I wish her experience would have been better.'

Same machine-transcript limitations as S01: unpunctuated, speaker-unlabelled, occasional garbling (a partner's name appears mangled and is therefore not quoted). sources.title: Rod Wave On Coping With Father 6 Year State Prison Bid and Regrets Stealing From Innocent People
sources.speaker: Rod Wave, interviewed by DJ Smallz Eyes
sources.locator: 29:21 interview, read via machine transcript. Key timestamps: 03:30-05:30 growing up in St. Petersburg; 06:30-09:00 father's six-year sentence and Uncle Derek stepping in then going to prison; 13:30-15:30 stealing to keep pressure off his mother; 17:30-22:00 the 2014 arrest and juvenile detention; 22:30-24:30 regret about the people he stole from.
sources.excerpt: He describes his early childhood as 'peaches and cream' while his father was making money, then the collapse after his father drew six years for charges he lists as including marijuana possession, attempted murder and tampering with a witness. He says he began breaking into cars and houses to keep financial pressure off his mother rather than out of any street ambition, and, asked about regrets (~22:54), answers 'I regret stealing from innocent people' (~23:07): he describes driving past those houses years later and wanting to knock on the door and apologise.
sources.context: The only substantial long-form interview in the packet from before he was famous: he was 19 or 20, two months into his Alamo deal and more than a year before 'Heart on Ice' charted. It is therefore the single most valuable check on whether the 2026 self-presentation is a promotional register or a durable pattern. Serious limitation: the 2018 machine transcript is of much poorer quality than the 2026 ones, with heavy garbling and profanity masking, so it is reliable for the substance of what he says but NOT at the sentence level. No direct quotation should be taken from it without listening to the audio. Draft stage 2026-09-17: transcript re-pulled; the regret passage ('I regret stealing from innocent people... ride past houses... wanna go knock on door') is confirmed in substance at ~23:07-24:10. Not cited in the current draft after cuts; retained as the only pre-fame long-form control source. Edit stage 2026-09-17: now cited in the temper section for his pre-fame statement of regret about stealing; the article paraphrases the substance rather than quoting the poor 2018 transcript at sentence level. Repair stage 2026-09-18 (verify-06): the research excerpt's 'single deepest regret' was a paraphrase with an unsupported superlative; the excerpt and the article now give his answer to 'any regrets' as said.

sources.title: Rod Wave Talks Going 'From The Nosebleeds To The Franchise Player Of The Team With Three Rings'
sources.speaker: Carl Lamarre, Billboard, with Rod Wave, Todd Moscowitz (Alamo Records CEO), Matt Ziegler and Tariq Cherif (Rolling Loud), Beau Williams (touring manager)
sources.locator: Full feature. Opening scene at Barclays Center, November 2023; biography section ('Rod Wave's first-ever performance...'); Alamo/Hit House section; Moscowitz and Rolling Loud quotes; fatherhood section; closing stadium/Grammy ambition.
sources.excerpt: Rod Wave: 'I went from the nosebleeds to the franchise player of the team with three rings.' On the staged fall from a ladder during 'Come See Me': 'That was from a dream I had... it's really to show people, Don't get up and do that when you can do this... Imagine [if] I would've [gone through with committing suicide]. I would've never made it to this part.' On fatherhood: '[Fatherhood] made me softer. Back then, I could just move and feel nothing. Now I feel like they made me a little weaker.' Todd Moscowitz: 'Rod pioneered this lane of struggle rap... He has half of the NFL in tears on Instagram when he drops a single'; 'His shows are like going to karaoke with 15,000 people.' 'Though Rod feared rejection, to his surprise, the video caught the attention of one of his football teammates.' Barclays: 'a sold-out audience of 12,000.'
sources.context: The only major reported magazine profile with on-the-record access to him and to his label, promoter and touring manager at once. Written at his commercial peak after three consecutive No. 1 albums. One verifiable factual error: it names his school 'Lakeview High School'; the Tampa Bay Times, his hometown paper, and Wikipedia both say Lakewood High School, and a 2017 Tampa Bay Times crime report places the pellet-gun lockdown at Lakewood High. It also dates his first-ever performance to a teammate's 2015 birthday party, which conflicts with the Tampa Bay Times account of an August 2016 first show. Beau Williams, quoted here approvingly as his touring manager, is the person his 2025 countersuit accuses of taking under-the-table payments.  Draft stage 2026-09-17: reopened and quoted passages matched against retrieved text.

sources.date: 2025-09-08 (posted); interview conducted after his 2025-08-29 Tampa show
sources.locator: Full Q&A. Intro paragraphs on the cancelled tour and Mainstay Touring; 'Why did you launch Mainstay Touring?'; 'How does it feel to be a star that operates in the mainstream...'; 'How far into the new album are you...'; the 'Sinners' origin answer; the Drake question.

'What even pushed me to want to be more hands-on with touring is just the fact that my last tour had to get taken down because of the routing.' We all got some sort of similarity.' 'I just kind of went and did it my own way... I just went with the flow. So I'm just way more comfortable. Whatever felt right, that's what I did.' Grizzly's complaint explicitly cites this interview as evidence that he was publicly blaming the promoter and announcing a competing tour in breach of an exclusivity clause, which makes it both a primary account and an exhibit in the litigation.  Draft stage 2026-09-17: reopened and quoted passages matched against retrieved text. Posted September 8, 2025; Grizzly sued on September 29, 2025. Repair stage 2026-09-18: now also used (C104) for the August 29, 2025 sold-out show at Tampa Bay's Benchmark International Arena, reported in the introduction, which contradicts the edit's 'gone for nineteen months'. sources.title: Rod Wave Recorded Alone in Dark Rooms For a Month to Make 'Pray 4 Love'
sources.speaker: Jessica McKinney, Complex, interviewing Rod Wave (age 21)
sources.locator: Full Q&A, conducted by phone during the first COVID lockdown. Key answers: the no-features question; 'What was the creative atmosphere like...'; 'Why have you chosen to go that route...'; 'Does it come naturally to write down emotions...'; the TikTok question; 'What do you want fans to take away...'
sources.excerpt: 'Making music for me is personal. When I do my music, I don't even go to the studio. It's just me and my engineer in a dark room somewhere, recording.' 'It really be personal for me... Music is a way of opening up. I don't really talk about it. I never thought I would be on the phone with you right now... I just wanted to make music, because it's how I get stuff off my chest. I want it to always feel like my escape.' 'I don't really discuss what I go through or how I feel. So by the time I sit down, it all comes up.' On 'Fuck the World': 'That's how I feel sometimes. I don't want to be around nobody, I just want to be alone.' 'Don't try to put me in the loop with the rappers... Don't look at me like a rapper, because I don't want to be treated like that.' 'If I feel like it was too personal, I ain't going to drop it.' 'The music is so personal that he decided not to rely on outside guest features.' 'I understand I'm a rapper, but I am a human. Just like you, I've got ups and down.'
sources.context: Six years before the 2026 interviews and at the very start of his mainstream success, with none of the mogul framing. The substance of the working method and the stated reason for it are almost identical to what he says in 2026, which is the strongest longitudinal corroboration in the packet. He also says here that he had no Instagram or Twitter before music and had not heard of TikTok while a song of his was going viral on it.  Draft stage 2026-09-17: reopened and quoted passages matched against retrieved text.

sources.title: How Rod Wave made it from St. Petersburg to music stardom
sources.speaker: Christopher Spata, Tampa Bay Times, reporting; with named testimony from Timmy Jenkins, Meghan Alfaro, Brandon Boyd (DJ Nephew), Andrew Lieber (booking agent), Erik Hill-Cainion
sources.date: 2021-09-22 (published); updated 2022-11-09; read via Internet Archive capture of 2024-04-09
sources.locator: Full feature. Backstage scene at MidFlorida Credit Union Amphitheatre, 2021-09-11; 'Thug Life' section on St. Petersburg; elementary chorus section; 'Pain' section on family; the 2014 arrest; Menage Lounge first show; Krispy Kreme; the closing scene with the child from the Children's Dream Fund.
sources.excerpt: 'This is all a fragment of the human orbit around Rod, who often sings of social anxiety and a need for solitude, with a track called Popular Loner on a mixtape titled PTSD. He did not speak with the Tampa Bay Times and does not do many interviews.' Booking agent Andrew Lieber, on Rod wanting to play the 2,000-capacity Jannus Live for his hometown show: 'I had to tell him, Rod, I'm sorry, you're too big.' After the biggest show of his life, to a boy with cancer: 'Is there anything I could have done better up there tonight?' he asks. 'I don't really know what to say between the songs.' On his engineer: 'He's never seen Rod write down a lyric.' Timmy Jenkins, elementary chorus classmate: 'I could never forget those days. We were old souls. We loved older music.' 'Rod and Lakewood classmate Elijah Simmons, a budding producer, started recording songs, but Rod was shy and uncomfortable with sharing anything publicly.' '"People are going to ride your wave," Simmons told him.' '"We call it the choir," says DJ Fizzumfade.' 'Rod is here, having arrived quietly at the last minute.' The engineer 'travels everywhere in case Rod wants to record at 4 a.m. in an Airbnb closet or an airport lounge.'
sources.context: The deepest independently reported account of his childhood, built from local records and people who knew him before the music, by his hometown daily. Crucially, it is reported without his cooperation, which both limits it and makes it the only substantial account in the packet not shaped by him or his label. It establishes the father's six-year sentence, Uncle Dee's federal sentence and roughly ten-year absence, the death of Uncle Dee's daughter Daijha at 17, the 2014 arrest and PTSD assessment, the August 2016 Menage Lounge debut at 17 for 500 dollars, the Krispy Kreme job and the eviction, and the 2020 Corvette crash. The original is behind a Tampa Bay Times subscription wall; it was read in full through the Internet Archive capture. Draft stage 2026-09-17: the Internet Archive capture was re-fetched and all quoted passages matched. Correction: the engineer's locations are an Airbnb closet or airport lounge, not hotel rooms. The draft links the original tampabay.com URL for readers; this record keeps the archive URL that was opened.

sources.title: Rod Wave Sued Over $27M 'Last Lap' Tour Advance, Allegedly Used It on 'Private Jets and Lavish Second Homes'
sources.speaker: Rachel Scharf, Billboard Pro, reporting on Grizzly Touring's federal complaint
sources.locator: Full article. Allegations on the $57m advance and 26 completed shows; the production-scale allegation; the citation of the September Billboard interview; the attached 2025-09-18 letter from Rod's attorney David Rose.
sources.excerpt: 'Grizzly allegedly advanced Rod $57 million to cover expenses like travel, lodging and production costs. But according to the lawsuit, Rod only completed 26 performances that earned $30 million against the guarantee, leaving $27 million in advances that he now won't repay.' From the complaint: 'Artist refuses to pay Grizzly a single penny of the more than $27 million he owes... and has instead chosen to spend his advance on private jets and lavish second homes.' 'Grizzly alleges that many Last Lap shows had to be canceled because Rod upped the scale of his tour production without warning, requiring more time to put up and take down his arena sets and making it impossible to play shows back-to-back as originally scheduled.'
sources.context: One side of an unresolved federal contract dispute, reported by Billboard's trade desk from the filing. These are allegations, not findings. The production-scale allegation is the only third-party account of why the tour broke, and it describes from the outside the same trait Rod describes from the inside when he says he is 'over creative' and calls every shot on his show.  Draft stage 2026-09-17: reopened and quoted passages matched against retrieved text. Filing date confirmed: 'a Monday (Sept. 29) federal court lawsuit'. The production-scale sentence is Billboard's paraphrase of the complaint.

sources.title: Rod Wave Countersues After $27M Tour Lawsuit: Promoter Is Trying to Force 'Indentured Servitude'
sources.speaker: Rachel Scharf, Billboard Pro, reporting on Rod Wave's counterclaims; quoting his lawyer James Sammataro and his representatives
sources.locator: Full article. The 'indentured servitude' quote; the routing allegations; the '12 of the 35' figure; the Beau Williams bribery allegation; the representatives' statement of 2025-10-13.
sources.excerpt: Billboard's own summary, not in quotation marks: Rod 'argues that Grizzly actually breached the contract by failing to properly load his touring equipment in and out of arenas and "making unilateral, onerous and inexplicable routing and booking decisions."' 'Rod contends in counterclaims filed Sunday (Oct. 12) that Grizzly's production failures and routing issues made it "logistically impossible" for him to complete the tour.' From the countersuit: 'Only 12 of the 35 scheduled [shows] occurred at the date and venue originally announced.' 'Rod says AG gave Williams at least $1.8 million in "under-the-table" payments so that the agent would underhandedly "sneak" a five-tour exclusively clause into the Last Lap tour contract. This plan was unsuccessful, says the countersuit, as Rod identified and rejected this exclusivity language.' 'Grizzly's lawyers did not immediately return a request for comment on Monday, nor did Williams.' His representatives: 'Grizzly Touring has no one to blame but itself.'
sources.context: The other side of the same unresolved dispute, again allegations rather than findings. Its importance to a personality reading is that it is the sharpest public act of blame in his record and it is aimed partly at his own former agent, six weeks after he told Billboard the tour was his to protect and a month before he told Shannon Sharpe he does not blame people.  Draft stage 2026-09-17: reopened and quoted passages matched against retrieved text. Filing date confirmed: 'counterclaims filed Sunday (Oct. 12)'. 'Indentured servitude' is lawyer James Sammataro's description of the relief Grizzly sought. Repair stage 2026-09-18 (verify-05): the load-in allegation is Billboard's paraphrase ('arenas'), not filing language; the article now labels it as Billboard's summary without quotation marks, and reports that the countersuit says the exclusivity scheme failed because Rod rejected the language. The Redemption Experience tour was announced to begin in December 2025 at Crypto.com Arena; whether it went ahead is not established.

sources.title: Rod Wave Steps Back From Music After Being 'Bashed' By Fans: 'I Don't FW You'
sources.speaker: Marisa Mendez, HipHopDX; quoting Rod Wave's Instagram post and Ari Lennox's Instagram Story
sources.locator: Full article. The 2025-01-28 Nashville cancellation; the hiatus post; the Ari Lennox statements about the 2023 Nostalgia Tour.
sources.excerpt: Rod Wave: 'To the rest of yall drag my name talk about me like a dog constantly speaking on me bashing me and what make me happy I dont fw you to the real fans that love me thank you this ain't goodbye it's simply see u later.' He also said he planned to 'travel, see the world, find love, raise kids, prolly go back to school.' Ari Lennox: 'Maybe I could've gotten over some of Rod Wave's evil, racist and demonic fans, but what made it even worse is Rod saying nothing in my defense. Privately or publicly.' Lennox also wrote: 'The only reason we met was because we ran into each in a Hotel Lobby after constant efforts of me trying to share my gratefulness for the opportunity.' claims.claim: In 2020 he told Complex music is personal and that he records with only his engineer in a dark room, and Complex reported that the music was personal enough that he decided not to rely on outside guest features.

The music was personal enough, Complex reported, that he "decided not to rely on outside guest features."
claims.inference: Complex reopened at draft stage; quotations verbatim. Edit stage: the draft's paraphrase "he skipped outside guest features" is replaced with Complex's own wording, because his catalogue does contain features and "skipped" overstated the solitude.
claims.alternative: Plenty of artists record without producers present, and he has released songs with guests. The distinctive element is the relational rationale and its persistence to 2026.

claims.claim: His January 2025 hiatus post addressed critics who 'drag my name... I dont fw you.'
claims.passage: his hiatus post was wounded, aimed at those who "drag my name" and ending "I dont fw you"

claims.claim: He released a mixtape titled PTSD with a track "Popular Loner", and his forearms are tattooed "Hard Times".

claims.claim: Charlamagne asked how someone whose music seems to carry so much pain became one of America's biggest artists without it destroying him.

claims.inference: Times reopened: 'He poses for photos with Julius, the boy with cancer from the Children's Dream Fund. "Is there anything I could have done better up there tonight?" he asks the boy. "I don't really know what to say between the songs."' Earlier the article describes 'a 15-year-old cancer patient whose greatest wish is to meet Rod Wave'; treating them as the same boy is a reasonable reading of the article's structure.

claims.claim: He calls the studio "my hobby, my therapy".
claims.passage: He calls the studio "my hobby, my therapy."

claims.passage: Of his own music at 19 he told Apple Music's The Plug Radio, "Damn, I was a little dramatic"

claims.passage: Rod has released seven studio albums, from _Ghetto Gospel_ in 2019 to _Don't Look Down_ in 2026
claims.inference: Wikipedia discography: Ghetto Gospel (2019), Pray 4 Love (2020), SoulFly (2021), Beautiful Mind (2022), Nostalgia (2023), Last Lap (2024), Don't Look Down (2026). Billboard confirms Ghetto Gospel as his first top 10 in 2019.

His October 2025 countersuit blames Grizzly's own load-in failures and its routing decisions. Both sides' claims are allegations, undecided in the coverage reviewed.

claims.claim: Description: Rod Wave says talking about his feelings is hard, so he puts them in songs arenas sing back.
claims.passage: Rod Wave says talking about his feelings is hard, so he puts them in songs arenas sing back.
claims.inference: Metadata summary of C21 and C54. Edit stage: the draft's "says he can't tell people how he feels" is softened to match what he actually describes, which is difficulty rather than incapacity.
claims.alternative: "So" compresses his own causal account into the description; the body attributes it to him.

claims.claim: The article's working definition of Type 9 is a person who declines to insist on their own significance.
claims.passage: What Nines decline to do is insist on their own significance, and Rod says it about himself.
claims.inference: Type description applied to the subject and immediately anchored to C17. Edit stage: the draft's "turning down the volume on their own presence" gloss was removed; it closely paraphrased the Type 9 definition in the linked Jelly-Roll profile, and the "peacemaker is not passive" reframe repeats two other Nine profiles in the comparison set.
claims.alternative: A general Enneagram description does no argumentative work by itself; the article now follows it directly with his own words rather than a metaphor.

claims.claim: Leading type reading: Type 9 at medium confidence, resting on which way he corrects a flattering frame. Type 4 is the strongest alternative and Type 8 is tested.
claims.passage: Rod Wave most likely fits Enneagram Type 9, at medium confidence. Offered any frame that makes him special, he flattens it: he rejects "pain" as the word for his music, asks to be seen as ordinary, and answers a grievance about awards by naming his own absence. Type 4 is the strongest alternative; Type 8 is also tested.
claims.inference: Summary of C26, C25, C23, C68 (the direction of his corrections) and C15/C93 (the awards answer). Edit stage: the draft's "declines grievances" was narrowed to the awards grievance, because the record holds several public grievances (C90, C37, C62).
claims.alternative: Circumstance explains much of the same behaviour without any type, and the article now says so in the type section itself rather than only in the biography.

claims.claim: The breakup answer describes a learned practice rather than an automatic pattern, so it is weighed as weak support for the Nine reading rather than as the decisive discriminator.
claims.passage: A practice learned in your twenties is weak evidence of a core motive, and has to be weighed against the type rather than counted as proof of it. What it is worth is the direction: handed a loss, he trained an exit rather than an argument.
claims.inference: Built on C28 and C29 as re-verified by the critic and enneagram reviewers. The draft called this "the sharpest" discriminator and named a heading after it; the fuller transcript shows a possessive, hard-hit baseline and a change that followed being left.
claims.alternative: A Four can also train detachment, and ordinary maturing explains it too. The article now ranks this third of three and states the transcript limits in the same paragraph.

claims.claim: The leading discriminator against Type 4 is the direction of his corrections: offered a frame that elevates him, he consistently flattens it, from 2020 to 2026.
claims.passage: A Four in that chair defends the significance of the feeling, because the feeling is the point. Rod hands it back, across six years and four outlets, including in 2020 when he had no reputation for calm to protect.
claims.inference: Applies C26 (Complex 2020), C25 (Billboard 2025), C23 and C68 (2026). Repair stage 2026-09-18 (verify-07): the 2020 Complex interview ran on the release day of Pray 4 Love, so there was an album to sell. What the 2020 material predates is the calmer-man album cycle of 2026 and any reputation for calm, which is what the article now says (C108) and what answers the durability objection that the type call rests on the August 2026 promotional window.
claims.alternative: Many Fours withhold rather than explain, so refusing to correct an image does not separate the types by itself; the article therefore rests the discriminator on the direction of the corrections he does make, not on his silence.

claims.claim: He calls himself "over creative", says he likes things done a certain way, and says he intends to call every shot.
claims.passage: He wants the controls, calls himself "over creative," says he likes "things done a certain way," and adds that he intends to call every shot.
claims.inference: Club Shay Shay ~14:26: "I'm over creative. I'm over I like things done a certain way... Like I'mma call all the shot." Said about business splits with labels. Edit stage: the draft used the first half only; the "call all the shot" clause is added because it is central to the Type 8 case the reviewers required.
claims.alternative: The context is creative and business control in a label deal, not personality in general. The draft's separate sentence linking this quotation to Grizzly's production allegation has been deleted; it backed one side of a live lawsuit with a quotation from an unrelated context.

claims.claim: He sounded similarly settled in a Billboard interview posted September 8, 2025, three weeks before Grizzly Touring sued him on September 29, 2025.
claims.passage: He sounded similarly settled to Billboard in September 2025, three weeks before Grizzly Touring sued him.
claims.inference: Billboard Q&A posted September 8, 2025; Grizzly suit filed September 29, 2025. Repair stage 2026-09-18 (verify-09): 'made the dispute public' is withdrawn, because the dispute was already public: the same Billboard piece reports the tour was cancelled 'due to production and routing issues', he blamed 'the routing' in it, and Grizzly's complaint cites the interview. The sentence now dates only the lawsuit. It still offers no inference about his state of mind from another party's filing.
claims.alternative: "Settled" characterises tone, and a public interview says little about private negotiations.

claims.claim: FAQ: asked in August 2026 whether he had been to therapy he said "Nah", then "Straight music, man"; he calls the studio his hobby and his therapy.
claims.passage: Asked by Charlamagne Tha God in an August 2026 Breakfast Club interview whether he had ever gone to therapy, Rod Wave answered "Nah." Asked if it was just music, he said, "Straight music, man." He describes the studio as his hobby and his therapy. That was his position as of August 2026.
claims.inference: Metadata restatement of C20 and C67. Edit stage: the question was changed from "Has Rod Wave ever been to therapy?" to "What has Rod Wave said about therapy?" and the answer now dates itself, because an FAQ answer is the surface most likely to be read as a current status years later.
claims.alternative: Same limits as C20.
claims.review_trigger: Review his long-form interviews at each album cycle, and no later than 2027-09-17, for any statement that he has started therapy or other formal support.

claims.claim: FAQ: Type 4 is the obvious reading of his music and of his own August 2026 account of a younger self who was 'so dramatic' and felt 'the world owed me something'; Type 9 leads on the direction of his corrections from 2020 to 2026.
claims.passage: Yes, and it is the obvious reading of his music, which is built on heartbreak and betrayal. In August 2026 he said that as a younger man he was "so dramatic" and felt "the world owed me something." The Type 9 reading still leads because of what he does when handed a flattering frame: from 2020 to 2026 he corrects toward the ordinary every time.
claims.inference: Metadata restatement of C58 and C76. Repair stage 2026-09-18 (verify-01): the edit's FAQ quoted 'my problems, my music, I'm sad, my this, my that' as his 'habit of mind'. That line comes from Club Shay Shay ~107:57-108:02, inside his answer to Shannon Sharpe's question (~101:41-103:43) about Lil Poppa's death and whether he had missed signs, directly after 'could I have done better, dog?'. It was self-reproach in grief, not a present self-description, and it is removed from the FAQ. The Four evidence the FAQ now uses is the Breakfast Club answer at ~28:40-29:02, where, asked what he has healed from, he says 'when I was younger I was so dramatic ... I felt like the world owed me something'.
claims.alternative: Same limits as the body discriminator. The 'so dramatic' answer is itself retrospective and framed as healing, so it supports a Four reading of his younger self more than of the present man.

claims.claim: FAQ: Type 9 at medium confidence, on the direction of his corrections; Type 4 strongest alternative, Type 8 also tested.
claims.passage: Rod Wave most likely fits Enneagram Type 9, at medium confidence. Handed a frame that would make him special, he flattens it: he rejects "pain" as the word for his music, asked in 2020 to be seen as "one of us making music," and answers a grievance about awards by naming his own absence. Type 4 is the strongest alternative, and Type 8 is tested too.
claims.inference: Metadata restatement of C74. Edit stage: the draft's "says he cannot talk about his feelings with people, only in songs" was removed as an overstatement of a limit he describes as partial (C21), and "declines grievances" was narrowed to the awards grievance.
claims.alternative: Same limits as the body argument.

claims.claim: His recorded material covers his father and Uncle Dee going to prison, Daijha's death from cancer, and being scared to love.
claims.passage: Few artists of his generation have put more private feeling on record: his father and then his father's friend "Uncle Dee" going to prison, a friend dead of cancer, being scared to love.
claims.inference: Lyrics quoted by the Times: "'Member pops went to prison, unc' took me inside. Then unc' went to prison" and "I lost Daijha to cancer, I just got over it. I'm scared to love, so scared to get close again." 'Few artists of his generation' is a comparative judgement, supported in spirit by Moscowitz's 'channels emotion and vulnerability in a unique way' and Billboard's 'sensitive confessionals'. Edit stage: "Uncle Dee" is now identified by role at first mention, for a reader who does not know who he is.
claims.alternative: The comparative is editorial and unquantified.

claims.claim: The article's reading is that speaking as himself, without a song to carry it, is the part of the job he avoids.
claims.passage: Speaking as himself, without a track underneath, seems to be the part of the job he avoids.
claims.inference: Supported by C66, C52, C21, C19. Edit stage: framed as the article's reading rather than asserted as fact, and narrowed to speaking without a track, because he gave three long interviews in three weeks in 2026 and the draft's flat "keeps avoiding" contradicted its own sources.
claims.alternative: He has given several long interviews and tours arenas, so any avoidance is partial and episodic.

claims.claim: At the 2021 Tampa show his fans recited every line, DJ Fizzumfade called them "the choir", and the Times reported Rod had arrived "quietly at the last minute".
claims.passage: Backstage, DJ Fizzumfade had a name for the fans who recite every line: "We call it the choir." Rod had arrived "quietly at the last minute," the Tampa Bay Times reported.
claims.inference: Times reopened at draft stage: "They'll recite every word. 'We call it the choir,' says DJ Fizzumfade"; "Rod is here, having arrived quietly at the last minute." Split out of C59 at edit stage because the opening paragraph was reordered. The article does not call Fizzumfade the tour DJ, since the Times mentions "Rod's tour DJ, a cousin" separately without confirming they are the same person.
claims.alternative: A reporter's scene; the late arrival may be ordinary headliner logistics. It opens the piece as a detail, not as proof.

claims.claim: He says he does not look for sympathy.
claims.passage: He declines help on principle: "I don't be looking for no sympathy," he told Sharpe.
claims.inference: Club Shay Shay ~109:20, verified at draft stage: "I don't be looking for no sympathy. For real... Like I'm going just deal with it myself because I feel like nobody really care about that kind of stuff cuz everybody dealing with their own problems." Split from C67 and moved into the Type 8 case, where the enneagram reviewer showed it fits an Eight's refusal of weakness at least as well as a Nine's self-effacement. Repair stage 2026-09-18: the second half of the quotation is cut for length; the retained fragment is verbatim.
claims.alternative: Common masculine reticence, and the practical risk of speaking freely while facing charges, both explain this without any type.

claims.claim: His breakthrough was "Heart on Ice", which went viral on TikTok and became his first Billboard Hot 100 hit; he told Complex in 2020 he had not heard of TikTok while it was happening.
claims.passage: His breakthrough, "Heart on Ice," went viral on TikTok and became his first Billboard Hot 100 hit; he told Complex in April 2020 that he had not heard of TikTok while it was happening.
claims.inference: Added after the fan reviewer noted the article never named the breakthrough its own sources are titled after ("'Heart on Ice' Rapper", Rolling Stone). The Tampa Bay Times and Billboard both record the TikTok virality and the Hot 100 entry; Complex records that he had not heard of TikTok while a song of his was going viral on it.
claims.alternative: Chart-debut ordinals depend on Billboard's records; the TikTok detail is his own account of his own ignorance, which is unusually cheap to verify against nothing.

claims.claim: Dereck Lane came home from federal prison and became Rod Wave's manager; he died in July 2024, and Revolt reported at the time that no cause of death had been revealed.
claims.passage: By then Uncle Dee had come home from federal prison and become his manager. Lane died in July 2024, seven months before the Last Lap tour fell apart; Revolt reported at the time that no cause of death had been revealed
claims.inference: Revolt/Rap-Up, July 3, 2024: 'At the time of reporting, a cause of death has yet to be revealed.' The Tampa Bay Times (2021) calls Lane his manager and Billboard (2023) has Lane designated as management. Repair stage 2026-09-18 (verify-08): the edit's present-tense 'no cause of death has been publicly released' is withdrawn. On Club Shay Shay (August 26, 2026, ~104:59-105:04) Rod said his uncle 'passed away the same way' as the younger rapper whose death he was discussing, while also saying he long could not believe it. That is his own grieving remark on air, not an official finding, and it is deliberately not used: the article dates the absence of a cause to Revolt's 2024 report and adds nothing about the manner of death.
claims.alternative: No official source in the packet has released a cause of death. Whether the loss bears on the 2024-2026 run is not claimed (C106).
claims.review_trigger: If a named official source releases a cause of death, revisit this sentence under suicide-reporting guidance. Do not add Rod's on-air characterisation.

claims.claim: He credits his father, who put him into football after Rod's own months in jail at 15, and Uncle Dee with his discipline, and says the tour collapse cost him focus on his kids and his health.
claims.passage: He credits his father, who put him into football after Rod's own months in jail at 15, with the discipline he says he still carries, and credits Uncle Dee with making him disciplined. He names the cost too: through the tour collapse, he told Sharpe, he could not focus on his kids or his health.
claims.inference: Added after the fan and enneagram reviewers showed the draft called the engine unexplained while he has explained it repeatedly. Billboard 2023: after he got out of jail his father put him in football, "a lot of discipline I learned then that I carry with me now." Club Shay Shay ~23:00-23:55 on Uncle Dee, and ~26:25 on what the collapse cost: "I couldn't even focus on certain stuff like my kids... My health." Paraphrased rather than quoted, because these runs come from an automatic transcript. Repair stage 2026-09-18 (verify-06): Billboard 2023 says he 'was charged with armed robbery at 15. After spending several months in jail, his father looked to instill discipline in him' and quotes 'when I got out of jail, he put me in football'. The jail was Rod's own, so the article now says so instead of the ambiguous 'after prison'.
claims.alternative: Self-reports do not settle motive, and a man explaining his own drive has an interest in a creditable origin. The point stands anyway: the gap is in the type theory, not in the public record.

claims.claim: He is the father of twin daughters and told Billboard in 2023 that fatherhood "made me softer".
claims.passage: He is the father of twin daughters, and told Billboard in 2023 that fatherhood "made me softer. Back then, I could just move and feel nothing."
claims.inference: Added after the fan reviewer noted the draft quoted his plan to "raise kids" without mentioning that he already had children. The Tampa Bay Times (2021) and Billboard (2023) report twin daughters, and Billboard quotes the "made me softer" line verbatim.
claims.alternative: The number and timing rest on two reported accounts; the article gives no birth date and names no child.

claims.claim: In January 2021 he attacked his label Alamo publicly on Instagram over money and a delayed album, and kept working with Alamo afterwards.
claims.passage: in January 2021 attacked his label publicly over money and a delayed album
claims.inference: Added after the fan, critic and enneagram reviewers all flagged that the packet held an opened source the draft never used, and that it undercuts both "declines grievances" and the draft's "lawyers litigate" explanation for the countersuit, since no lawyers were involved here. HipHop-N-More, February 2021, quotes the Instagram Story. Billboard 2023 shows Alamo still his label two years later.
claims.alternative: A blog-tier outlet quoting posts that are no longer live and were not independently viewed. The article reports the fact and the continued partnership without reproducing the profanity, and the later "everything cool" post was not found on reopen, so it is not claimed.

claims.claim: He says he begins from distrust: "I start off by not trusting nobody."
claims.passage: He starts from suspicion: "I start off by not trusting nobody."
claims.inference: Club Shay Shay ~48:42-48:52, listed in the S01 locator at draft stage and quoted by the critic and enneagram reviewers. Added because it is one of the clearest lines for the control- and autonomy-centred alternative the draft never tested.
claims.alternative: Said about the music industry, where distrust is ordinary prudence rather than temperament.

claims.claim: In a grieving answer on Club Shay Shay he said that while the Last Lap tour was collapsing he had been absorbed in his own problems and felt people should be telling him it would be okay, used The Fault in Our Stars to make the point that everybody is going through something, and said that situation woke him up.
claims.passage: In a long, grieving answer on Club Shay Shay, he looked back at the stretch when the Last Lap tour was collapsing. He had been absorbed in his own problems, he said, and felt "people should be telling me it's going to be okay." He reached for _The Fault in Our Stars_, whose heroine in his telling feels "the world just revolve around her," to make the opposite point, "everybody going through something," and said "that situation really woke me up."
claims.inference: The question he was answering: at ~101:41-101:47 Sharpe raises the death of Lil Poppa, a younger rapper on the Last Lap tour (S19 confirms the death), and at ~103:34-103:43 asks whether there were signs he missed. The whole run to ~108:45 is that answer, and it mixes grief for Poppa and for his uncle with self-reproach. The lines used sit at ~105:55-106:51: the film comparison (~105:55-106:12, 'the world just revolve around her'), 'Everybody going through something, bro' (~106:23, a Rod turn that runs straight into his account of the tour), 'I'm dealing with I'm my problems is what's going on' (~106:36-106:39, paraphrased as 'absorbed in his own problems'), 'People should be telling me it's going to be okay' (~106:41-106:43), 'everybody going through something' again (~106:44-106:47), and 'that situation really woke me up' (~106:48-106:51), followed by 'you got to check on your strong friends'. Repair stage 2026-09-18 (verify-01, fan-06): the edit called these lines 'unprompted', presented 'my problems, my music, I'm sad, my this, my that' as his present 'habit of mind' and ranked them the strongest Four evidence. That line (~107:57-108:02) follows 'could I have done better, dog?' about Poppa and is ambiguous in the auto transcript (it may describe his music, which Poppa 'loved'); it is no longer quoted anywhere. The passage now says the answer was grieving and retrospective, and gives the self-correction he drew from it. No death is named in the article, because the subject and critic reviewers showed that naming it beside his distance implies culpability; 'grieving answer' and 'self-reproach after a loss' carry the context instead. 'That situation' is quoted, not glossed, because the transcript does not settle whether it means the tour or the death. Speaker turns in this run come from an automatic transcript; the ambiguous '>> Like, it's not this about me' at ~106:21 is not quoted because it may be Sharpe's.
claims.alternative: Self-absorption during the worst weeks of a career, and self-reproach after a friend's death, are ordinary for anyone. That is why the article counts the passage for neither type (C109).

claims.claim: In the same awards answer he says trophies were never part of his character and that what he cares about is his worth on paper; in 2023 he named Grammys as a goal, he was nominated in November 2025, and in 2026 he said he is starting to network more.
claims.passage: But in the same answer the trophies have "just never been part of my character," which makes giving them up cost nothing, and he swaps in another scoreboard: "Long as they know my worth on paper... that's all I care about." In 2023 he told Billboard his goals were stadiums and "Grammys and sh-t." He was nominated for one in November 2025, and in 2026 said he is "starting to network more."
claims.inference: Added after the fan and critic reviewers showed the draft presented the awards answer as a costly test that he passes, while omitting the evidence that it costs him nothing and that he has voiced open ambition. Club Shay Shay ~5:54-8:45; Billboard December 2023 for the stadiums-and-Grammys goal; Rolling Stone for the November 2025 nomination.
claims.alternative: Giving up something he says he never wanted is not a costly choice. The article now says the awards test fails rather than passes, and does not replace it with another untested one.
claims.review_trigger: If he wins a major award, or campaigns for one, revisit this passage and the awards line in the type answer and FAQ.

claims.claim: He says that once he was older the same promoters kept booking him and he began staying and socialising at the clubs.
claims.passage: He also said that once he was older the same promoters kept booking him and he stayed and hung out, so the rule did not outlast the constraint that made it.
claims.inference: Club Shay Shay ~120:46-120:56, raised by the critic reviewer. Added because the draft called waiting in the car "a rule he chose to keep" while the same answer says he stopped keeping it, which turned a constraint on a minor into a lifelong disposition.
claims.alternative: His own retrospective account again. It limits the anecdote rather than extending it, which is why it is included.

claims.claim: He took the SoFi promotion partly to prove a point: "no matter what you do, you cannot take that from me."
claims.passage: He declines to prove who he is, then takes a stadium promotion deal so that "no matter what you do, you cannot take that from me."
claims.inference: DancehallMag, reopened at draft stage: "let me show these people what I can do. And now no matter what you do, you cannot take that from me." Set against C19's "try to prove a point of who I am". The enneagram reviewer identified this split as either a real discriminator or a real unexplained item; the article treats it as the discriminator and repeats the gap in the closing.
claims.alternative: A man announcing a new business has reason to talk about proving himself. The split between proving what he can do and proving what he is is the article's inference, stated as such.

claims.claim: He says the trained detachment made him a better person because a partner should be treated as a privilege whose feelings matter.
claims.passage: He also says the lesson was relational, that it "made me a better person" because you should "treat it like it's a privilege to be with somebody."
claims.inference: Club Shay Shay ~68:30-69:40, quoted by the subject, critic and enneagram reviewers. Added because the draft kept only the part about protecting his work ethic, which made a stated relational lesson read as cold detachment.
claims.alternative: A flattering gloss on detachment, offered by a man in a relationship on a friendly show. It is included because omitting it made him sound colder than the source does.

claims.claim: He says his adolescent anger came out in dangerous ways that put him in situations he could not get out of, before music became the outlet.

type_hypothesis.against:
Four things resist the Type 9 reading.

First, he has grievances and he airs them. In January 2021 he attacked Alamo publicly over money and a delayed album, with no lawyer involved (C90). In January 2025 the same post that said goodbye to his fans told his critics he did not care for them (C39, C62). In August 2026, asked why he founded Mainstay, he blamed the Last Lap partners at length before offering the line about not blaming people (C37). His public account and his filing agree. What remains is that a man described as declining friction fights often. Repair narrowed the article's answer: his documented disputes ran through a post, a withheld album, a filing and a post, but Eights post and sue too, so the form of his fights weighs lightly (C99).

Second, the engine and the appetite for control (C45, C46, C69, C77, C91, C95, C102). Seven studio albums in eight years, a touring company founded after a catastrophe, a promoter role on Ye's SoFi shows taken to prove a point, "I just wanted to be in control", "I'mma call all the shot", "I start off by not trusting nobody". He explains where the discipline came from (C88), so the gap is in the type rather than in the record. Nine theory does not predict a man who declines to prove who he is and then sets out to prove what he can do.

Third, anger and its costs. His father warns him about his temper (C43); he says his adolescent anger came out in dangerous ways (C44, C97). The public record holds a 2014 juvenile shooting case (C05) and three adult cases alleging violence: the 2021 misdemeanor battery surrender after a promoter said Rod hit him (C41), the dropped 2022 domestic battery charge (C40), and the denied May 2025 Fulton County case including aggravated and simple assault and pointing a gun (C42). A November 2025 drug and weapons case alleges no violence (C107). None is proven, and the article draws no inference from any of them in either direction; only his own statement about his anger is used. Separately, Lennox says he said nothing in her defense (C38), which is a cost of the pattern rather than evidence against it.

Fourth, the source base (C53). Three of the most quoted sources were recorded within three weeks in August 2026 to promote one album, every quotation from them was checked against automatic transcripts rather than audio, and there is no adversarial profile and no neutral long-acquaintance witness. Circumstance (a father and father figure imprisoned, a friend's death, legal exposure, an industry that rewards mystique) explains much of the same behaviour without any type, and the article concedes that inside the type argument (C101).
type_hypothesis.alternative_case:
Type 4 remains the strongest alternative. The catalogue runs on heartbreak and betrayal; he released a mixtape titled PTSD with "Popular Loner" and has "Hard Times" tattooed on his forearms (C64). He describes his younger self in Four terms: "when I was younger I was so dramatic ... I felt like the world owed me something... how could they do that to me?" (C58, used in the FAQ, C80). He says betrayal marked him more than poverty because betrayal is a decision (C56). His January 2025 hiatus post is wounded (C62). His untrained response to loss was possessive and hard-hitting (C29). A Four reading explains the dark rooms as protection of an inner life too personal for collaborators, awards indifference as disdain for a system that cannot see him, and the career as a wound made into identity.

Repair stage 2026-09-18: the edit had called his August 2026 Club Shay Shay lines ("people should be telling me it's going to be okay", "my problems, my music, I'm sad, my this, my that") the strongest, unprompted Four evidence. They come from his grieving answer about a younger tourmate's death and whether he missed signs, and the same answer turns to "everybody going through something". The article now presents them in that context (C92) and counts them for neither type (C109); the ambiguous "my problems, my music" line is no longer quoted.

Type 8 was also tested at the reviewers' insistence (C100), on the strength of the control, distrust, temper and blame material. It is not adopted, for the reasons in the discriminator, but it is not dismissed either: it fits his business conduct better than Type 4 does, and the discriminator against it is moderate rather than decisive. Type 5 is noted and set aside, since nothing in the record shows a Five's hoarding of knowledge or energy. The Barclays Center ladder fall, which the draft used as Four evidence, was removed because Billboard records his stated purpose for it as a message to fans about suicide.
type_hypothesis.discriminator:
The leading discriminator is the direction of his corrections (C76). Handed a frame that would make him larger, he flattens it, and he was doing it years before the calmer-man album cycle of 2026 (C108): in 2020, at 21, "I understand I'm a rapper, but I am a human. Just like you", and a request to be seen as "one of us making music" (C26); in 2025, "I'm not like a superstar or a fairy tale" (C25); in 2026, a refusal of the word "pain" for his own material, "it's not pain, it's not sad ... it's normal. It's reality" (C23), and "Damn, I was a little dramatic" about his own nineteen-year-old records (C68). What a Four defends is the significance of their own feeling. Rod hands it back, across six years and four outlets. The split that makes this more than modesty is what he will insist on: he declines to prove who he is (C19) and takes a stadium promotion so that "no matter what you do, you cannot take that from me" (C95). He will prove what he can do; he will not prove what he is.

The second discriminator is aimed at Type 8 (C99), and repair narrowed it (verify-04). Its stronger half is the pre-fame record: two outlets describe a teenager "shy and uncomfortable with sharing anything publicly" who "feared rejection" (C60), and after graduation he denied his own stage name to a customer at a Krispy Kreme drive-thru (C09). Its weaker half is that his documented disputes with his label, promoter and critics ran through an Instagram post and a withheld album (C90), a court filing (C36) and a post (C62); Eights post and sue too, so this weighs lightly. The edit's "never face to face" and "nineteen-month absence" are withdrawn: the untested allegations of physical violence (C40, C41, C42) count neither way, and the post-January-2025 step back lasted about two months before new music (C104, C105). This separates Nine from Eight only moderately, which is part of why confidence stays at medium.

The third, the breakup answer, is ranked last and labelled weak (C28, C29, C75). By his own account in the same run, the detachment is a practice he trained after somebody left before he was ready, over a possessive, hard-hit baseline, and he says the lesson was relational rather than self-protective (C96). A learned practice is weighed against the type, not counted as proof of it. What it is worth is the direction: handed a loss he trained an exit rather than an argument.

Demoted to corroboration or excluded: the uncorrected public image cuts both ways, because he names the mystique as a "plus" (C19). His picture of peace does not distinguish anything, because almost anyone describes rest as a bed and a clean house (C30). The awards answer fails as a costly test, because he says trophies were never part of his character and swaps in another scoreboard (C15, C93). The grief passage is counted for neither type (C92, C109). Confidence stays at medium for these reasons, and because circumstance explains the distance about as well as the type does (C101).
type_hypothesis.unexplained:
1. The engine and the appetite for control. He has explained where his discipline came from (C88), but no type account explains a man this reluctant to insist on himself wanting every control and taking a stadium deal to prove a point (C45, C46, C95, C102).

2. How direct his conflicts really are. His documented business and public disputes ran through posts and filings (C99), but three adult cases allege physical violence (C40, C41, C42), none tested in the coverage reviewed. The article cannot say which picture is complete and counts the allegations neither way.

3. The violence-related, weapons-related and drug charges between 2014 and 2025, all dropped, denied or undecided in the coverage reviewed, with no public explanation (C05, C40, C41, C42, C103, C107). The article draws nothing from them.

4. Whether the settled voice of August 2026 is change or register. He sounded similarly settled in September 2025, three weeks before Grizzly sued him (C53, C78).

5. What Dereck Lane's death in July 2024 bore on the tour's collapse and the pause that followed (C87, C106). The article states the sequence and does not claim a link, because no source establishes one.
